title: Belief-State Memory for Partially Observable Multi-Agent Workflows
research_question: Can a shared belief-state memory that explicitly tracks alternative task hypotheses and their confidence improve end-to-end accuracy and reduce unnecessary agent interactions in partially observable multi-agent workflows?
hypothesis: Compared with standard message-passing orchestration, a belief-state memory layer that preserves multiple plausible task states and updates them during monitor-analyze-plan-execute cycles will reduce coordination errors caused by premature commitment, yielding higher task success at lower communication cost.
motivation: The knowledge base highlights a concrete gap around model-selection uncertainty: existing adaptive systems work argues that choosing a single best model can create overconfident, brittle decisions, while the rejected workflow ideas cluster around routing, debate depth, escalation, and verifier allocation rather than explicit representation of competing workflow hypotheses. This suggests an unexplored angle for agentic workflow optimization: importing belief maintenance from self-adaptive systems into multi-agent orchestration so agents coordinate over structured uncertainty instead of committing early to one decomposition or interpretation.
